title: Shared site release raised complete delivery and total failure in eight selected worm circuit models
abstract: We tested one-step transmission from each source neuron to its targets in eight public worm brain maps. We compared independent contact release with one release event shared by all targets at each site. Both models keep each target success probability fixed. A conditional proof shows that shared release cannot reduce complete delivery and cannot reduce total failure. In a fixed 162-cell panel, 140 to 143 source neurons per map had retained sites. At release probability 0.3, the equal-source mean gain in complete delivery was 0.66 to 6.34 percentage points. The loss in delivery to at least one target was 0.78 to 16.25 points. Monte Carlo bounds for complete delivery were at most 0.070 points, with simultaneous nominal 95 percent coverage across 24 map and probability settings. The direction held at release probabilities 0.1 and 0.5. Shared release can help a task that needs all recipients and harm a task that needs any recipient. These are conditional model results. Brain site release dependence was not measured. Partial maps, uncertain target labels, a selected cell panel and unmatched animals prevent a claim about biological reliability or age effects. Raw and source-level data remain outside this baseline publication.

display.caption: Shared minus independent all-target success, and independent minus shared any-target success. Values are equal-source means. Error bars bound Monte Carlo error, not biological uncertainty. Maps are different animals with unequal age spacing.
